cur:manuscripts-aethelwold-entry-jerusal.summary: Within a frame of luxuriant 'Winchester' acanthus with gold bosses at the corners, Christ rides astride a donkey toward the city, followed by a crowd carrying golden palm branches; two youths at the gate spread their mantles under the donkey's feet, while figures lean from the walls and climb a tree to throw branches. The picture faces the blessing for Palm Sunday.
facts: The Benedictional of St Æthelwold, written by the monk Godeman for Bishop Æthelwold of Winchester (963–984), is regarded as the masterpiece of late Anglo-Saxon illumination; it has 28 full-page miniatures.
The British Library describes this page as the preface to the blessing for Palm Sunday.

cur:manuscripts-urgell-beatus-lamb-victo.summary: In a starry sky above, the Lamb with a halo and cross-staff stands triumphant, while below, on a red ground, the beasts and the serpent lie overthrown with their human-headed riders. The text 'Explanatio supra scripte storie' begins beneath the picture. The page shows the promise that the Lamb shall overcome the powers of evil, 'for he is Lord of lords, and King of kings'.
facts: The Beatus of Urgell has 90 illustrations; it names no scribe or painter, but is thought to come from the same scriptorium as the Valcavado Beatus and to date from the late 10th century.
The manuscript has been recorded at La Seu d'Urgell since 1147.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-87-christ.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, holding a book and attended by angels and the sun and moon, sits on a globe and inclines his ear toward the leprous psalmist, who stretches out his arms to him from a sarcophagus set in a pit into which streams flow. Other sarcophagi surround him. 'I am counted with them that go down into the pit' is drawn with stark literalness.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-87-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-santa-cecilia-apse.summary: Against a deep blue sky with red-edged clouds, Christ stands at the centre on a cloud, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a scroll, while the hand of God crowns him from above. He is flanked by Saints Paul, Cecilia and Pope Paschal I (with the square halo of the living, holding a model of the church) on one side and Peter, Valerian and Agatha on the other; below, the twelve lambs process from Bethlehem and Jerusalem. The composition deliberately recalls the 6th-century apse of Santi Cosma e Damiano.
facts: Pope Paschal I rebuilt the church in 822 and moved the relics of Saint Cecilia here from the Catacombs of Saint Callixtus.
Paschal I appears in the mosaic with a square halo, the conventional sign that the person was still alive when the image was made.

cur:objects-ringelheim-crucifix.summary: This monumental wooden figure of the crucified Christ hangs with arms stretched straight out, his body upright, head slightly bowed, wearing a long loincloth. The calm, dignified figure shows a Christ who reigns from the cross even in death. Together with the Gero Cross in Cologne it is one of the earliest large-scale crucifixes of the Middle Ages.
facts: German Wikipedia records that Bishop Bernward of Hildesheim gave the monumental crucifix to the convent of Ringelheim, where his sister Judith was abbess around 1000, possibly on the occasion of her death.
cur:objects-ringelheim-crucifix.notes: Material details beyond 'wood' are not verified. The photo shows the crucifix as displayed in the Hildesheim Dommuseum (2019).

vam:O88286.summary: Two miracles of healing are carved one above the other. In the upper scene Christ, followed by four disciples, reaches out to a leper whose limbs are covered with sores; in the lower, accompanied by two apostles, he touches the eyes of a blind man who is led forward by three helpers. The compact, rounded figures and the frame of foliage are typical of ivory carving at Metz in the later 9th century.
facts: This plaque and the Transfiguration plaque in the V&A (256-1867) appear to have been made together, probably for a book cover.
Melzak connected both plaques with the later Metz ivories on the border of the 'Cathedra Petri', the throne in St Peter's, Rome, and dated them to 870–880 (V&A).
The background is extremely thin and cracked; pin-holes in the corners were for fixing the plaque to a backing.
vam:O88286.notes: V&A: Carolingian, France, Lorraine (Metz), ca. 870–880. Purchased from Webb.

Q22084482.summary: Seated on a hillside, Christ raises one hand as he teaches a gathered crowd of men, women and children, their faces absorbed in his words. The Danish painter Carl Bloch made it as one of 23 scenes from the life of Christ for the King's Oratory at Frederiksborg Castle, and its gentle, dignified Christ has become one of the most familiar images of Jesus in the modern world.
facts: Bloch's 23 paintings for the King's Prayer Chamber (oratory) beside the Frederiksborg Castle Chapel were painted between 1865 and 1879 and remain there today.
For decades, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has used Bloch's Frederiksborg paintings extensively in its chapels, manuals and publications.
Bloch largely avoided conventional halos, wings and other traditional Catholic motifs, which has been suggested as one reason his work appealed so widely to Protestant and Latter-day Saint audiences.
Bloch lived in Italy from 1859 to 1866, and the etchings and paintings of Rembrandt, which he studied closely, were a major influence on his art.
